+# Working notes — programmes fed by the ml-ensemble-extremes card
+
+Card: does 10–1,000 AIFS-ENS members beat 50 for top-percentile wind/temperature/rain
+probabilities, or does shared model error (exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained
+distribution) cap the skill? Test runs AIFS-ENS v1, 7 dates x 1,000 members, scores
+top-percentile fields vs ERA5 with fair CRPS + Brier, checks whether skill rises past 50.
+
+## Programme 1 — ECMWF, AIFS ENS (operational machine-learned ensemble)
+- This is the direct target. The card reproduces AIFS-ENS v1 (afCRPS) and sweeps 10–1,000 members.
+- Operational model page / model card: https://huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-ens-2.0
+- Science paper (AIFS-CRPS): https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15832 ; journal: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44387-026-00073-7
+- Step targeted: member generation (exchangeable draws) + verification of extreme-event skill + the operational
+  ensemble-size choice. Today: 51 members (50 + control), N320, 15-day, 4x/day; scored as 50-member ensembles vs IFS.
+- Key quotes:
+  - "The trained model is stochastic and can generate as many exchangeable members as desired and computationally feasible in inference." (arxiv 2412.15832 abstract)
+  - "It is run operationally by ECMWF, generating a 51-member 15-day (6-hourly) global forecast four times per day." (HF card)
+  - "We compare 50-member 15-day AIFS-CRPS ensemble forecasts with the 9-km 50-member ECMWF IFS (Integrated Forecasting System) ensemble forecasts." (nature)
+  - "An important next step is the assessment of the forecast skill of extreme events. Here, CRPS can have limited sensitivity to tail properties of distributions." (nature)
+  - "a single member 15 day forecast is created in about one minute for AIFS-CRPS O96 and four minutes for AIFS-CRPS N320 on an NVIDIA A100 40 GB GPU, including the time spent reading the initial state and writing the forecast to disk." (nature) — the card's reproduction target.
+- Activity: active. "The ensemble model has been running operationally since 1 July 2025 and was upgraded from AIFS ENS v1 to AIFS ENS v2 on 12 May 2026." (https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/datasets/aifs-machine-learning-data)
+- Already done? partly. ECMWF has done ensemble-size convergence for the physics-based IFS ensemble (Leutbecher 2017,
+  up to 200 members), not for AIFS-ENS exchangeable members; extreme-event skill explicitly flagged as next step.
+  - https://www.ecmwf.int/sites/default/files/elibrary/2017/17621-ensemble-size-how-suboptimal-less-infinity.pdf
+    "50 and 200 members are 2% and 0.5% worse than ∞ , respectively"
+
+## Programme 2 — HENS (Huge ENSembles), NVIDIA Earth-2 / SFNO project
+- The card's "closest prior" [s_hens]. HENS already ran a 7,424-member huge ensemble but with a different
+  ensemble-generation scheme (bred vectors + 29 independently trained SFNO checkpoints = genuine model uncertainty),
+  not exchangeable draws of a single afCRPS-trained distribution.
+- Recipe home (current, maintained): https://github.com/NVIDIA/earth2studio/tree/main/recipes/hens
+- Paper: https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/18/5605/2025/
+- Step targeted: huge-ensemble generation + tail/outlier sampling for extreme events.
+- Key quotes:
+  - "HENS uses customized bred vectors for initial condition perturbations and multiple independently trained model checkpoints to represent model uncertainty, specifically designed for better representation of extreme weather events." (recipes/hens README)
+  - "Here in Part 2, we generate a huge ensemble (HENS), with 7424 members initialized each day of summer 2023." (GMD)
+  - "Here, we combine these two perturbation techniques to create a 7424-member ensemble: 256 initial condition perturbations for each of the 29 SFNO checkpoints." (GMD)
+  - "The 7424-member ensemble has an information gain of 4. This means that HENS is large enough to have at least one ensemble member that is 4 standard deviations away from the ensemble mean (on average)." (GMD)
+  - "We use this estimate of 7000 to guide our choice of ensemble size for HENS." (GMD)
+- Activity: active. Earth2Studio v0.19.0 released 2026-09-30 (https://github.com/NVIDIA/earth2studio/releases/tag/0.19.0).
+- Already done? partly — analogous experiment but SFNO-BVMC, not AIFS-ENS exchangeable draws.
+
+## Programme 3 — Anemoi (ECMWF open-source ML weather framework, co-developed with European NMS)
+- Where AIFS-ENS is actually run/reproduced (anemoi-inference) and where verification tooling lives.
+- https://github.com/ecmwf/anemoi ; inference: https://github.com/ecmwf/anemoi-inference ; core: https://github.com/ecmwf/anemoi-core
+- Step targeted: running AIFS-ENS ensemble inference (reproducing member runtime/memory) + evaluation/verification tooling.
+- Key quotes:
+  - "As an 'end to end' framework, it provides a comprehensive toolkit that spans data preparation, model training, and inference, enabling meteorological organizations to leverage their own data for ML-based weather prediction." (github ecmwf/anemoi README)
+  - "AIFS ENS v2 is implemented using the Anemoi framework. Anemoi consists of open source components, enabling the user community to run AIFS themselves." (HF aifs-ens-2.0 card)
+  - "Run evaluation pipelines for data-driven weather models built with Anemoi." (https://github.com/MeteoSwiss/evalml)
+  - "These ensemble scores assess spatial structure across graph neighbourhoods, edge differences, global fields, variables (global energy) and spectral amplitudes" (anemoi-core commit 11e8498e, "graph scores", 2026-08-20)
+- Activity: active. anemoi-core released graphs v0.9.8 / training-0.17.1 on 2026-10-01; anemoi-inference pushed 2026-10-16.
+- Already done? no — Anemoi is tooling; it has not run the 10–1,000-member AIFS-ENS extreme-tail saturation experiment.
+
+## Gaps
+- Nobody has run the exact experiment: 10–1,000 exchangeable AIFS-ENS (afCRPS) members scored for top-percentile
+  wind/temp/rain vs ERA5. ECMWF's ensemble-size work is for physics-based IFS; HENS's is for SFNO-BVMC.
+- AIFS-ENS v2 (12 May 2026) swapped afCRPS for a multi-scale loss; members are still exchangeable draws, so a v1
+  result would need re-checking on v2 before changing practice.

"Here is a research card, written to answer this root question: Do more members of a machine-learned weather ensemble buy better forecasts of rare extremes, or does error shared by all members cap the skill?

**ml-ensemble-extremes · Ensemble size for rare extremes in a machine-learned weather ensemble.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever · PASS

**Question.** Does 10 to 1,000 AIFS-ENS members beat 50 for top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain probability forecasts, or does shared model error cap the skill?

**What is known.** HENS Part 2: 7,424 SFNO members per day for 92 summer-2023 dates; showed huge ensembles sample 4-sigma tails and reduce outliers. Whether AIFS-ENS, whose members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, keeps gaining skill past 50 members or saturates from shared model error.

**Hypothesis.** More members keep helping: 1,000 members sample top-percentile tails far better than 50, so extreme-event scores keep improving [s_hens].

**If compute is the lever.** Skill on top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain keeps rising past 50 members: 1,000 members sharpen the tails and improve extreme-event scores.

**If not.** Skill flattens near 50 members: members are exchangeable draws of one trained distribution, so shared model error caps tail sharpness and extra members add nothing.

**Test.** Run 7,000 fifteen-day AIFS-ENS v1 forecasts (7 dates x 1,000 members) on eight A100 40 GB GPUs; subsample 10-1,000 members, score top-percentile wind/temperature/rain probabilities against ERA5 with fair CRPS and Brier scores, and test whether skill still rises past 50 members.

*Compute axis.* Ensemble members per forecast: 10–1,000 members, 6 levels. Closest prior: 7,424 [s_hens], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Reproduce the published 4-minute N320 member time and 38 GB memory; one control run must match ECMWF open data within ensemble spread [s_crps_paper]. Tolerance: timing within +/-25% of 4 min; 38 GB memory fits; control field within the ensemble's own member-to-member spread at each lead time (GPUs are non-deterministic, so exact reproduction is not expected).

**Would not show.** Applies to AIFS-ENS v1 medium-range extremes on 7 dates; not a multi-season reforecast, other models, subseasonal leads, or direct proof that shared error causes any saturation.

*Cost.* Plans $963.17 of the $1,000 budget over 74.3 machine-hours, leaving $36.83. Main guess: peak filesystem usage [g], measured after $19.90 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 15× higher. Full scale: A 30-date multi-season reforecast at 1,000 members, $3,980, 3.98× the budget.

# Description of the upgrade

The operational release of AIFS ENS v2 will introduce scientific and architectural changes to the AIFS ensemble model.

- The introduction of a new wave component, including 11 wave variables, marking ECMWF's first operational data-driven wave forecasts.
- The addition of a new snow variable to the existing land component.
- The addition of 2 variables already present in AIFS Single (vsw and cp), to harmonise the two models.
- An improved representation of the stratosphere, with the addition of pressure level fields at 10hPa.

For real-time files transmitted via ECMWF's dissemination service (ECPDS):

- Changes to the priority of data files
- Changes to the default file-naming convention of data files

Architectural changes include:

- Replacing the afCRPS loss function used in AIFS ENS v1 with a multi-scale loss. See https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.10868.
- Imposing the same variable bounding as is used by the AIFS Single model, improving physical consistency.
- Revised graph features, utilising more edges in the decoder.
- An improved training regime, using 1 years of additional training data compared to AIFS ENS v1.

...

# Description of the model

The upgrade of AIFS ENS to version 2 introduces changes to the training regime and model architecture. 

The full training procedure for AIFS ENS v2 consists of:

- Pre-training, which remains the same as for AIFS ENS v1

- Pre-training is performed on ERA5 data covering the years 1979–2022 over 300,000 training steps.
- Fine-tuning, which has been updated for AIFS ENS v.2

- Fine-tuning is performed on years of additional data compared to AIFS ENS v1.0. In particular, fine-tuning is performed on ECMWF operational analysis data and available IFS 50r1 esuite analysis data, covering the years 2018-2024 over 7,900 training steps. 
- As in previous versions of AIFS ENS, IFS fields are interpolated from their native O1280 resolution (approximately 0.1°) using MARS default interpolation tools down to N320 (approximately 0.25°) for fine-tuning and initialisation of the model during inference. 

For both phases of training, a cosine learning rate schedule and a batch size of 16 is used. 

Further model changes include introducing a multi-scale loss and removing reference field truncation, imposing the same variable bounds used by the AIFS Single model to improve physical consistency, and revising graph features by using more edges in the decoder together with new edge features.

AIFS ENS v2 is implemented using the Anemoi framework. Anemoi consists of open source components, enabling the user community to run AIFS themselves. A model card and demonstration notebook are available on Hugging Face.

# Significant update to ECMWF’s key forecasting systems IFS and AIFS goes live

12 May 2026 

 

A significant upgrade to ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System (IFS), Cycle 50r1, has gone live today (12 May 2026) alongside an update to the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS v2).

Cycle 50r1 introduces a more consistent and integrated approach to forecasting the atmosphere’s interactions with the ocean through fully coupled data assimilation, and improvements to known issues with accurately forecasting sudden, heavy, localised rain. It also brings more advanced representation of waves and sea ice.

The update to the AIFS introduces, among other features, ECMWF’s first data-driven wave and snow cover forecasts.

Florian Pappenberger, Director-General of ECMWF, said: “This is an important upgrade for ECMWF and for everyone who relies on our forecasts. IFS Cycle 50r1 strengthens our physics-based forecasting system, including through fully coupled atmosphere–ocean–sea-ice assimilation and new ocean and sea-ice capabilities.

...

"With AIFS v2, we are expanding its performance, bringing a new generation of AI forecasting into operation, building on ECMWF’s technical competence, operational expertise and data

...

For AIFS, both the Single and Ensemble versions of the system are being upgraded to version two, with each introducing a new wave component. 

Eleven wave-related variables are being made available to users, enabling predictions, for example, of when we will experience rougher seas. In addition, the AIFS Single v2 wave component shows substantial improvement in the medium-range skill of wave forecasts compared to the physical model, IFS Cycle 50r1.

ECMWF’s first data-driven snow cover forecasts are also being introduced with this upgrade. Again, the AIFS Single v2 forecasts show improved performance compared to IFS Cycle 50r1 forecasts, with the predicted snow cover fraction closer to observations.

# AIFS ENS v2 

 

The AIFS is ECMWF's Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System. It consists of two data-driven medium-range forecast models:

- AIFS Single v2 (described on the following page)
- AIFS ENS v2 (described here)

AIFS ENS v2 was implemented on 12 May 2026 and supersedes version 1. It is run operationally by ECMWF, generating a 51-member 15-day (6-hourly) global forecast four times per day.

...

## What's new in v2 

The release of AIFS v2 introduces:

- A new wave component, including 11 wave variables, marking ECMWF's first operational data-driven wave forecasts.
- The addition of a new snow variable to the existing land component.
- The addition of tropical cyclone track forecasts.
- The addition of two variables already present in AIFS Single (vsw and cp), to harmonise the two models.
- Improved vertical velocities, by changing parameter W from a prognostic to a diagnostic field.
- An improved representation of the stratosphere, with the addition of pressure level fields at 10hPa.

Architectural changes include:

- Replacing the afCRPS loss function used in AIFS ENS v1 with a multi-scale loss.
- Imposing the same variable bounding as is used by the AIFS Single model, improving physical consistency.
- Revised graph features, utilising more edges in the decoder.
- An improved training regime, using 1 year of additional training data compared to AIFS ENS v1.

For full details of the changes introduced with this upgrade, see the implementation page

...

### Access AIFS Single v2 model data 

ECMWF generates operational forecasts from AIFS ENS v2 four times per day (at 00, 06, 12 & 18 UTC). Users can access the forecast data free-of-charge through various open data platforms.

...

### Model description 

AIFS ENS v2 is based on a graph neural network (GNN) encoder and decoder, and a sliding window transformer processor.

 

The model has a flexible and modular design and supports several levels of parallelism to enable training on high resolution input data. AIFS forecast skill is assessed by comparing its forecasts to numerical weather prediciton (NWP) analyses and direct observational data.

- Developed by: ECMWF
- Model type: Encoder-processor-decoder model
- License: Inference model weights are published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). To view a copy of this licence, visit https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. The demonstration notebook and other script files are published under an Apache 2.0 licence. To view a copy of this license, visit https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.txt.

...

AIFS ENS v2 is trained on ECMWF’s ERA5 re-analysis and ECMWF’s operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) analyses as described in the training data section.

AIFS ENS v2 is trained to produce 6-hour forecasts. It receives as input a representation of the atmospheric states at $t−6ht_{−6h}$ t− 6 h​, $t0t_{0}$ t 0​, and then forecasts the state at time $t+6ht_{+6h}$ t+ 6 h​.

...

#### Speeds, Sizes, Times 

Data parallelism is used for training, with a batch size of 1. One model instance is split across two 120GB GH200 GPUs, with an ensemble instance split across 4 gpus. Training is done using mixed precision (Micikevicius et al. [2018]), and the entire process takes about one week, with 32 GPUs in total. The checkpoint size is 2.55GB and as mentioned above, it does not include the optimizer state.

Over the last few years, several machine-learned weather prediction models have emerged that show superior per formance to that of traditional physics-based models in many forecast scores. The first generation of these models produced deterministic predictions and were trained to minimise a mean-squared-error (MSE) loss [Pathak et al., 2022, Bi et al., 2023, Lam et al., 2023, Chen et al., 2023, Lang et al., 2024a]. The MSE training objective incentivises the smoothing of forecast fields with lead-time and a reduction of forecast activity, to avoid the ’double-penalty’ incurred when forecasting misplaced structures (e.g. Hoffman et al. [1995], Ebert et al. [2013]). Nevertheless, evaluations demonstrated that these models display surprisingly physical behaviour in classical forecast situations [Hakim and Masanam, 2024], and provide genuine, useful predictions, including of many extreme events [Ben Bouallègue et al., 2024a]. The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) is now producing semi-operational weather predictions using the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS, Lang et al. [2024a]) four times per day. For the usefulness of a weather forecast it is important to account for forecast uncertainties. Ensemble forecasts are run to estimate the probability density of the atmospheric state at a future time [Lewis, 2005, Leutbecher and Palmer, 2008]. In physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP), this is achieved via running the forecast model from a range of perturbed initial conditions and by introducing stochastic perturbations into the forecast model itself. The aim is to generate a well calibrated ensemble. This means that on average, the ensemble standard deviation needs to match the root-mean square error of the ensemble mean (e.g., Fortin et al. [2014]), and the predicted probability of an event should accurately reflect the observed probability of it occurring. For physics-based ensemble simulations with the Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) at ECMWF [Molteni et al., 1996a], initial condition uncertainty is represented via an ensemble of data assimilations [Buizza et al., 2008, Isaksen et al., 2010, Lang et al., 2019] and singular vector perturbations [Leutbecher and Palmer, 2008]. Perturbations to the initial conditions of the ensemble members are then constructed from both (see Lang et al. [2021] for an up-to-date description of the initial perturbation methodology). Uncertainties associated with the forecast model are represented stochastically [Leutbecher et al., 2017, Berner et al., 2017]. For the first generation of machine-learned weather prediction models, ensemble forecasts were mainly based on an ensemble of MSE trained forecast models [Bihlo, 2021, Scher and Messori, 2021, Clare et al., 2021, Pathak et al., 2022, Bi et al., 2023, Weyn et al., 2024]. The resulting ensemble forecasts tend to have too little ensemble spread. This is in line with the models having difficulties to represent the inherent variability of the atmosphere due to their training regime [Ben Bouallègue et al., 2024b]. The second generation of machine-learned weather forecast models are based on probabilistic training. For example, Kochkov et al. [2024] developed a hybrid model that combined a differentiable solver for atmospheric dynamics with a machine-learned physics module; this approach achieved good ensemble scores. Most notably, denoising diffusion [Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015, Karras et al., 2022] has been used successfully to create machine-learned ensemble models that are competitive with physics-based NWP models across a range of probabilistic forecast scores [Price et al., 2023, Lang et al., 2024b, Alexe et al., 2024a]. Next to providing useful information about forecast uncertainties, these models have more stable statistics than the deterministically trained models and do not smooth out small-scale structures with forecast lead time. This can make forecasts more stable, and in some cases allows for consistent simulations from months [Alexe et al., 2024a] to many years [Kochkov et al., 2024]. At ECMWF, the first approach towards a machine-learned ensemble model is also based on a diffusion approach [Lang et al., 2024b, Alexe et al., 2024a] that achieves competitive ensemble scores when compared to the physics-based 9 km IFS ensemble [Lang et al., 2023]. In this work, we take a different approach: we introduce AIFS-CRPS, a machine-learned ensemble forecast model that is based on optimising a probabilistic proper score objective, similar to Pacchiardi et al. [2024], Shokar et al. [2024] and Kochkov et al. [2024]. AIFS-CRPS learns how to represent model uncertainty, through shaping Gaussian noise. For training, we use the almost fair continuous ranked probability score (afCRPS), a modification to the fair continuous ranked probability score (fCRPS) [Ferro et al., 2008, Ferro, 2013, Leutbecher, 2019]. AIFS-CRPS is a highly skilful machine-learned ensemble forecast model that is competitive or superior to the physics based IFS ensemble across forecast lead times ranging from days to subseasonal predictions.

Ensemble weather forecasts provide a probabilistic description of the future state of the atmosphere and give users flow-dependent estimates of forecast uncertainty. Here, we introduce AIFS-CRPS, an ensemble variant of the machine-learned Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS) developed at ECMWF. Its loss function is the almost fair Continuous Ranked Probability Score (afCRPS). It is based on a proper score, the CRPS, but approximately removes the bias in the score due to finite ensemble size yet avoids a degeneracy of the fair CRPS. The trained model is stochastic and can generate as many exchangeable members as desired. For medium-range forecasts AIFS-CRPS outperforms the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) ensemble for the majority of variables and lead times. For subseasonal forecasts, AIFS-CRPS outperforms the IFS ensemble before calibration and is competitive with the IFS ensemble when forecasts are evaluated as anomalies to remove the influence of model biases.

...

At ECMWF, the first approach towards a machine-learned ensemble model is also based on a diffusion approach 28 that achieves competitive ensemble scores when compared to the physics-based 9 km IFS ensemble 29. In this work, we take a different approach: we introduce AIFS-CRPS, a machine-learned ensemble forecast model that is based on optimising a probabilistic proper score objective, similar to refs. 30, 31 and 24. AIFS-CRPS learns how to represent model uncertainty, through shaping Gaussian noise. Its loss function is based on the CRPS 32, a univariate proper scoring rule. For training, we use the almost fair continuous ranked probability score (afCRPS), a modification to the fair continuous ranked probability score (fCRPS) 33, 34, 35, which approximately removes the bias in the score due to finite ensemble size yet avoids a degeneracy of the fair CRPS (see section 4.2). CRPS is a well-established scoring rule widely used for ensemble verification, hence it is a natural choice as the basis for a loss function. The approach requires only a single model evaluation per forecast step, making it computationally more efficient than diffusion-based methods which typically require multiple denoising steps. In training, proper score optimisation allows for the model to be rolled out over multiple forecast steps.

...

AIFS-CRPS is a machine-learned ensemble forecast model that is highly skillful across forecast lead times ranging from days to subseasonal predictions. Unlike deterministic machine-learned weather models that are trained to minimise mean-squared error, AIFS-CRPS is trained probabilistically using a proper scoring rule based on the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), enabling it to generate stochastic forecasts that maintain realistic atmospheric variability. The model can produce as many exchangeable ensemble members as required from a single trained model. Each member is generated via independent random perturbations.
